quizTitle: Technopreneurship - Module 6: Production Planning and Control

questions.text: Production Planning and Control (PPC) is defined as the strategic engine that translates a high-tech prototype or code architecture into what?
options: A frozen design ready for million-unit replication
A funded business plan approved by investors
A patented and fully protected intellectual property
A scalable, commercially viable market product
questions.explanation: PPC is the strategic engine that translates a high-tech prototype or code architecture into a scalable, commercially viable market product.

questions.text: What is the primary focus of Traditional Industrial PPC?
options: Validating demand through pilot group signals
Deploying evolving tech before cash runs out
questions.explanation: Traditional Industrial PPC focuses on maximizing high-volume factory efficiency, reducing overall cost per unit, and optimizing steady-state operational workflows.

questions.text: Which of the following are listed as the primary focus of Traditional Industrial PPC?
questions.explanation: Traditional Industrial PPC targets high-volume efficiency, lower cost per unit, and steady-state workflows. Runway, deployment time and pivoting belong to technopreneurial PPC.

questions.text: Technopreneurial PPC is described as being driven by what?
options: Economies of scale and frozen designs
questions.explanation: Technopreneurial PPC is driven by survival, agility and extreme uncertainty.

questions.text: Which limited critical startup resources does Technopreneurial PPC coordinate?
questions.explanation: Technopreneurial PPC coordinates three limited critical startup resources: capital and financial runway, human talent and core expertise, and time to deployment.

questions.text: What is the ultimate goal of Technopreneurial PPC?
options: Secure steep volume discounts by buying raw materials in bulk
Make the exact same item millions of times as cheaply as possible
Deploy evolving tech without running out of cash before achieving Product-Market Fit
Keep machines and labor running at 90%+ capacity at all times
questions.explanation: The ultimate goal is to deploy evolving tech without running out of cash before achieving Product-Market Fit.

questions.text: Before spending capital, which questions does Production Planning answer?
options: What are we building, how will we build it, and when do we scale?
How do we adapt to immediate disruptions while preserving our runway?
Who owns the intellectual property built during the project?
How do we make this product 2% cheaper than last year?
questions.explanation: In Production Planning (the vision and strategy), the technopreneur acts as an architect to answer: what are we building, how will we build it, and when do we scale?

questions.text: Once the green light is given, which question does Production Control answer?
options: Which tier of contract manufacturer should we launch with?
How many subscribers do we need to break even each month?
How do we adapt to immediate disruptions while preserving our financial runway?
What are we building, how will we build it, and when do we scale?
questions.explanation: Production Control (the execution and adaptation) acts as the real-time radar to answer: how do we adapt to immediate disruptions while preserving our financial runway?

questions.text: Match each part of PPC to the role the technopreneur or the process plays in it.
allChoices: Acts as an architect before spending capital
Acts as an auditor after the product ships
Acts as the real-time radar once the green light is given

pairs.match: Acts as an architect before spending capital
Acts as the real-time radar once the green light is given

questions.explanation: In planning, the technopreneur acts as an architect before spending capital. In control, the process acts as the real-time radar once the green light is given.

questions.text: Match each Production Planning and Production Control area to its focus label.
questions.explanation: Planning: Agile Demand Forecasting (Market Signals), Design for Manufacturing (Scalability), Routing & Sourcing (Resource Optimization). Control: Shop Floor & Micro-batch (Process Agility), Dynamic Inventory Tracking (Lean Stock), Bottleneck & Burn-Rate (Risk Remediation).

questions.text: Why does Agile Demand Forecasting not rely on historical sales data?
options: Investors prohibit using past data in pitch decks
Historical data only applies to software products
A tech startup does not have historical sales data
Historical data is too expensive to buy from vendors
questions.explanation: Instead of relying on historical sales data, which a tech startup does not have, planning relies on pre-orders, crowdfunding metrics, or pilot group signals.

questions.text: Which signals does Agile Demand Forecasting rely on?
questions.explanation: Agile Demand Forecasting relies on market signals: pre-orders, crowdfunding metrics, or pilot group signals, since a startup has no historical sales data.

questions.text: In Production Planning, what does DFM stand for?
questions.explanation: DFM stands for Design for Manufacturing, the Scalability area of Production Planning.

questions.text: What does Design for Manufacturing (DFM) map out?
options: Which components are made in-house and which are contracted to overseas vendors
How many days capital is trapped in raw materials before returning as revenue
How software loops or electronic components scale from single bench prototypes to thousands of units
How minor engineering adjustments are pushed out mid-production without stopping
questions.explanation: DFM maps how software loops or electronic components scale up from single bench prototypes to thousands of units seamlessly. The other options describe Routing & Sourcing, Shop Floor & Micro-batch, and the C2C cycle.

questions.text: A startup decides to build its firmware in-house but contract the enclosure to a specialized regional vendor to keep initial asset costs low. Which Production Planning area is this?
questions.explanation: Routing & Sourcing (Resource Optimization) is deciding what components to make in-house versus contract out to overseas or specialized regional vendors, to keep initial asset costs low.

questions.text: What does the Shop Floor & Micro-batch area of Production Control do?
options: Maps how prototypes scale up to thousands of units seamlessly
Pushes out minor engineering or software adjustments mid-production without stopping the entire line
Solves problems in real time when microchips get delayed at customs
Keeps buffer stock minimal because tech parts can become obsolete overnight
questions.explanation: Shop Floor & Micro-batch (Process Agility) is pushing out minor engineering or software adjustments mid-production without stopping the entire line.

questions.text: Why does Dynamic Inventory Tracking keep buffer stock minimal (Just-In-Time)?
options: Tech parts can become obsolete overnight or market demands can pivot drastically
Suppliers refuse to sell large quantities to startups
Investors require all inventory to be sold within one month
Warehouses in the Philippines charge high storage fees
questions.explanation: Dynamic Inventory Tracking (Lean Stock) keeps buffer stock minimal because tech parts can become obsolete overnight or market demands can pivot drastically.

questions.text: Custom microchips get delayed at customs and the startup's server cloud capacity maxes out. Which Production Control area handles this?
questions.explanation: Bottleneck & Burn-Rate (Risk Remediation) is real-time problem solving when custom microchips get delayed at customs or a server cloud capacity maxes out.

questions.text: According to The Paradigm Shift, what is the primary goal of Technopreneurship PPC?
options: Minimize storage space and handling overhead
Minimize unit cost via extreme replication
questions.explanation: Technopreneurship PPC aims to maximize learning rate and speed-to-market. Traditional manufacturing aims to minimize unit cost via extreme replication.

questions.text: What tooling setup does Technopreneurship PPC use?
options: Soft/flexible tooling, such as 3D printing and CNC machining
Fully automated assembly lines from day one
Heavy upfront tooling, such as steel molds
Rigid tooling locked in by long-term vendor contracts
questions.explanation: Technopreneurship PPC uses soft/flexible tooling (e.g., 3D printing, CNC machining). Traditional manufacturing uses heavy upfront tooling (e.g., steel molds).

questions.text: In The Paradigm Shift, what are the material risks in Traditional Manufacturing PPC?
options: Component obsolescence and sudden product pivots
questions.explanation: Traditional manufacturing's material risks are storage space and handling overhead. Technopreneurship's are component obsolescence and sudden product pivots.

questions.text: In The Paradigm Shift, what are the material risks in Technopreneurship PPC?
options: Idle machines and low equipment effectiveness
Component obsolescence and sudden product pivots
questions.explanation: Technopreneurship PPC's material risks are component obsolescence and sudden product pivots.

questions.text: Classify each element from The Paradigm Shift as belonging to Traditional Manufacturing PPC or Technopreneurship PPC.

pairs.term: Minimize unit cost via extreme replication

questions.explanation: Traditional: minimize unit cost via replication, heavy upfront tooling, storage/handling risks, rigid long-term vendor contracts. Technopreneurship: maximize learning rate and speed-to-market, soft/flexible tooling, obsolescence/pivot risks, a hybrid, fluid contract manufacturing ecosystem.

questions.text: In a traditional manufacturing setup, what is the primary goal?
questions.explanation: In traditional manufacturing, demand is predictable and design is frozen, so the primary goal is Economies of Scale: making the exact same item millions of times as cheaply, quickly, and flawlessly as possible.

questions.text: How are market demand and product design described in a traditional manufacturing setup?
options: Demand is uncertain but the design is entirely frozen
Demand is predictable but the design is constantly evolving
Demand is predictable and the design is entirely frozen
Demand is uncertain and the design is constantly evolving
questions.explanation: In a traditional setup, market demand is predictable and the product design is entirely frozen.

questions.text: In traditional manufacturing PPC, Overall Equipment Effectiveness, abbreviated ___, is paramount.
questions.explanation: The traditional metric of success is Unit Cost & OEE (Overall Equipment Effectiveness). If a machine sits idle, money is being lost.

questions.text: "If a machine sits idle, money is being lost." Which traditional PPC metric of success does this describe?
questions.explanation: Under Unit Cost & OEE, Overall Equipment Effectiveness is paramount: if a machine sits idle, money is being lost.

questions.text: What does the traditional core strategy of "Diluting Fixed Costs" involve?
options: Offloading production to a global contract partner after traction
Scheduling massive production runs to dilute fixed costs like expensive steel molds or automated assembly lines
Scheduling micro-batches so a failed design doesn't waste capital on inventory
Syncing component orders with investor funding tranches
questions.explanation: Traditional PPC's core strategy (High Upfront Investment) is Diluting Fixed Costs: scheduling massive production runs to dilute fixed costs like expensive steel molds or automated assembly lines.

questions.text: Whose philosophy is this? "We know exactly what the customer wants. Our job is to build it with zero waste and maximum speed."
questions.explanation: This is the Traditional Manufacturing PPC philosophy (Zero Waste & Speed), which assumes demand is known and the design is frozen.

questions.text: Whose philosophy is this? "We think we know what the customer wants, but we need to test it immediately. Our factory must be flexible enough to change tomorrow."
questions.explanation: This is the Technopreneurship PPC philosophy (Rapid Testing), since a startup faces extreme uncertainty about what the market wants.

questions.text: In a tech startup, what is the primary goal of PPC?
options: Economies of Scale: making the same item millions of times as cheaply as possible
High Utilization: keeping machines and labor at 90%+ capacity
Agile Validation: getting small batches to customers fast to learn what works before running out of money
Zero Waste: building a frozen design with maximum speed
questions.explanation: Because a startup faces extreme uncertainty and an evolving design, the primary goal is Agile Validation: getting small batches to customers fast to learn what works before running out of money.

questions.text: What is the metric of success in Technopreneurship PPC?
options: Volume discounts secured on raw materials
questions.explanation: Success is measured by Time-to-Market & Cash Runway Preservation: how fast you can build, measure, and pivot based on customer data.

questions.text: Why does Technopreneurship PPC schedule micro-batches?
options: So that machines can run at 90%+ capacity at all times
So that steel mold costs are spread over more units
So that if a design fails, capital isn't wasted on inventory
So that suppliers grant a 10% unit discount
questions.explanation: The core strategy is Micro-Batches with low upfront investment, so if a design fails, capital isn't wasted on inventory.

questions.text: Which of the following are given as ways Technopreneurship PPC produces micro-batches?
questions.explanation: Micro-batches use 3D printing, CNC machining, or flexible cloud software architectures. Steel molds, automated lines and bulk orders belong to traditional PPC.

questions.text: In the Strategic Comparison, what is the primary driver question of Traditional Manufacturing PPC?
options: How do we make this 2% cheaper?
How long until we run out of cash?
Which design should we pivot to next?
How do we get this to users next week?
questions.explanation: Traditional PPC's primary driver is Cost Reduction: how do we make this 2% cheaper? Technopreneurship's is Speed & Flexibility: how do we get this to users next week?

questions.text: In the Strategic Comparison, what is the primary driver question of Technopreneurship PPC?
options: How do we get this to users next week?
How do we make this 2% cheaper?
How do we secure steeper volume discounts?
How do we keep every machine running?
questions.explanation: Technopreneurship PPC's primary driver is Speed & Flexibility: how do we get this to users next week?

questions.text: What is the "nightmare scenario" for Technopreneurship PPC?
options: A Machine Breakdown: stopping a high-speed assembly line that costs thousands per minute
A Customs Delay: custom microchips held at the port for weeks
A Supplier Price Hike: losing a 10% volume discount
The Wrong Product: spending 6 months perfectly mass-producing an item nobody wants to buy
questions.explanation: Technopreneurship's nightmare is The Wrong Product (6 months mass-producing an item nobody wants). Traditional manufacturing's nightmare is A Machine Breakdown.

questions.text: Match each strategic dimension to how Traditional Manufacturing PPC views it.
questions.explanation: Traditional PPC: Cost Reduction (make it 2% cheaper), A Machine Breakdown (a stopped line costs thousands per minute), inventory as an Asset/Buffer bought in bulk, and High Utilization (90%+ capacity). Technopreneurship's matching views are Speed & Flexibility, The Wrong Product, Liability/Risk and Excess/Fluid Capacity.

questions.text: In Technopreneurship PPC, inventory is viewed as an asset/buffer, so raw materials are bought in bulk to secure steep volume discounts.
questions.explanation: That is the traditional view. Technopreneurship PPC views inventory as a Liability/Risk: materials are kept tight (Just-In-Time) because tech components become obsolete fast.

questions.text: Under Traditional Manufacturing PPC's High Utilization capacity focus, at what level must machines and labor run at all times?
questions.explanation: High Utilization means machines and labor must be running at 90%+ capacity at all times.

questions.text: What does the Excess/Fluid Capacity focus of Technopreneurship PPC mean?
options: Running machines and labor at 90%+ capacity at all times
Buying extra raw materials to protect against shortages
Keeping setups modular so production can instantly scale up, down, or pivot
Building a second factory before demand is proven
questions.explanation: Excess/Fluid Capacity means keeping setups modular so production can instantly scale up, down, or pivot.

questions.text: Match each Core Pillar of Technopreneurial PPC to its description.
allChoices: Aligns production schedules strictly with funding disbursements
Plans production in distinct stages matching fundraising milestones
Treats the bill of materials as alive and flags how engineering changes alter costs and timelines

pairs.match: Treats the bill of materials as alive and flags how engineering changes alter costs and timelines
Plans production in distinct stages matching fundraising milestones
Aligns production schedules strictly with funding disbursements

questions.explanation: Pillar 01 manages a living BOM, Pillar 02 scales production in stages matching fundraising milestones, and Pillar 03 aligns schedules with funding disbursements to preserve runway.

questions.text: In Dynamic BOM Management, BOM stands for Bill of ___.
questions.explanation: BOM stands for Bill of Materials. Pillar 01 is Bill of Materials (BOM) Lifecycle Management.

questions.text: Why is a product's bill of materials described as "alive" in technopreneurship?
options: A change in an electronic sensor's availability can break the entire enclosure design
It is updated automatically by the government every quarter
It must be rewritten whenever a new investor joins
Suppliers can legally change prices without notice
questions.explanation: In technopreneurship, the BOM is alive: a change in an electronic sensor's availability can break the entire enclosure design.

questions.text: What does Technopreneurial PPC use digital, integrated environments for under Dynamic BOM Management?
options: To negotiate minimum order quantities with suppliers
To file patents for every new component used
To instantly flag how engineering changes alter component costs and production timelines
To replace contract manufacturers with in-house automated lines
questions.explanation: Technopreneurial PPC leverages digital, integrated environments to instantly flag how engineering changes alter component costs and production timelines.

questions.text: Match each stage of Modular Stage Scaling to what happens in it.
allChoices: Offloading to a global contract partner once consumer traction justifies the investment
Short batches using temporary tooling to test marketplace feedback

pairs.match: Short batches using temporary tooling to test marketplace feedback
Offloading to a global contract partner once consumer traction justifies the investment

questions.explanation: Stage 1 (Alpha/Beta) is single-unit hand-assemblies for lab testing. Stage 2 (Pilot Run) is short batches of 10 to 100 units on temporary tooling. Stage 3 (Mass Customization) offloads to a global contract partner once traction justifies it.

questions.text: How many units are in a Pilot Run Stage batch?
questions.explanation: The Pilot Run Stage uses short batches of 10 to 100 units, with temporary tooling, to test marketplace feedback.

questions.text: Modular Stage Scaling plans production in distinct stages that match what?
questions.explanation: Startups cannot afford automated assembly lines on day one, so production is planned in distinct stages matching fundraising milestones.

questions.text: The Alpha/Beta Stage uses temporary tooling to produce short batches that test marketplace feedback.
questions.explanation: The Alpha/Beta Stage is single-unit hand-assemblies for lab testing. Short batches (10 to 100 units) using temporary tooling describe the Pilot Run Stage.

questions.text: Complete the quote from Pillar 03: "In technopreneurship, ___ is the ultimate constraint."
questions.explanation: Cash Runway Alignment: "In technopreneurship, cash is the ultimate constraint."

questions.text: Traditional PPC optimization targets machine uptime. What must hardware startups subordinate machine efficiency to?
questions.explanation: Hardware startups must subordinate machine efficiency to liquidity, aligning production schedules strictly with funding disbursements.

questions.text: What is the Capital Freeze Risk?
options: A machine breakdown stops the high-speed assembly line for 3 months
Investors freeze funding until the product reaches Product-Market Fit
A key chip goes out of stock and freezes the production planning cycle
The master schedule delivers parts 3 months prior to assembly, prematurely locking up critical working capital
questions.explanation: The Capital Freeze Risk: if the master schedule delivers parts 3 months prior to assembly, it prematurely locks up critical working capital.

questions.text: What is the impact of the Capital Freeze Risk?
options: It cancels the startup's NTC certification
It deprives marketing and R&D teams of vital funds required to keep the startup operational
It forces the factory to run below 90% capacity
It voids the startup's patent filings
questions.explanation: Locking up working capital early deprives marketing and R&D teams of vital funds required to keep the startup operational.

questions.text: What is the Technopreneurial PPC solution to the Capital Freeze Risk?
options: Synchronize material drops and component orders precisely with investor funding tranches and capital cycles
Buy all components in bulk early to lock in a 10% discount
Delay assembly until every part has been in storage for 3 months
Switch to a Tier 1 manufacturer immediately
questions.explanation: Material drops and component orders are synchronized precisely with investor funding tranches and capital cycles, maximizing runway without compromising assembly timelines.

questions.text: Match each part of The Startup Sourcing Mix (Make vs. Buy vs. Hack) to its framework.
questions.explanation: Contract Manufacturing is CM Selection, the Hybrid Framework is BYOP (Bring Your Own Parts), and Rapid Prototyping is The MVP Ecosystem (rapid fabrication services).

questions.text: In the startup sourcing mix, the hybrid framework is called BYOP, which stands for Bring Your Own ___.
questions.explanation: BYOP stands for "Bring Your Own Parts", the hybrid sourcing framework.

questions.text: What does the BYOP (Bring Your Own Parts) framework involve?
options: Using rapid fabrication services for short-run productions
Evaluating Tier 1 and Tier 3 contract manufacturers by capital constraints
Letting customers supply their own replacement parts after purchase
Procuring long-lead-time or critical custom silicon components independently and shipping them directly to assembly partners
questions.explanation: BYOP manages procurement risks for long-lead-time or critical custom silicon components independently, shipping them directly to assembly partners.

questions.text: On what basis does CM Selection evaluate and negotiate with contract manufacturing partners?
options: Brand popularity and social media following
Number of patents the CM holds
questions.explanation: CM Selection evaluates and negotiates with appropriate contract manufacturing partners based on production scale and capital constraints.

questions.text: Which of the following are given as examples of rapid-turnaround fabrication services in The MVP Ecosystem?
questions.explanation: PCBWay (electronics) and Protolabs (injection molding) are the rapid fabrication services. OpenBOM and Propel are cloud PLM tools, ESP32 is a pre-certified RF module, and Raspberry Pi is open-source hardware for testing jigs.

questions.text: Match each rapid fabrication service to what it is used for.
questions.explanation: PCBWay is the example for electronics and Protolabs for injection molding.

questions.text: According to The Technopreneur's Dilemma, starting directly with a Tier 1 manufacturer is:
options: Recommended for pilot runs of 10 to 100 units
The safest way to iron out design defects cheaply
Almost always a mistake, and usually impossible due to capital constraints
Required before applying for NTC certification
questions.explanation: Starting directly with a Tier 1 manufacturer is almost always a mistake, and usually impossible due to capital constraints.

questions.text: What is the risk of relying entirely on a Tier 3 shop long-term?
options: Tier 3 shops require heavy steel tooling from day one
Tier 3 shops refuse to collaborate on engineering changes
It makes the startup ineligible for government grants
It can limit your ability to scale when your product experiences explosive market adoption
questions.explanation: Relying entirely on a Tier 3 shop long-term can limit your ability to scale when your product experiences explosive market adoption.

questions.text: Why should a startup launch its initial MVP and pilot runs at a Tier 3 manufacturer?
options: Tier 3 manufacturers offer the lowest possible unit cost at high volume
Tier 3 manufacturers handle global mass customization
Proximity, lower financial risk, and engineering collaboration let you iron out design defects without burning through cash
Tier 3 manufacturers are the only ones allowed to use 3D printing
questions.explanation: Launch at Tier 3 ("Low Risk & Engineering Collaboration"): proximity, lower financial risk, and engineering collaboration let you iron out design defects without burning through cash.

questions.text: Which conditions should be in place before scaling from Tier 3 to a Tier 2/1 partner?
options: A signed NDA with one pilot customer
A first batch of crowdfunding pre-orders
questions.explanation: Scale to Tier 2/1 ("Verified Fit & Cost Reduction") once you have verified product-market fit, stable engineering designs, and predictable high-volume demand, then use your manufacturing data to slash unit costs.

questions.text: When transitioning to a larger tier partner, what does the startup leverage to slash unit production costs?
questions.explanation: Once fit, designs and demand are verified, the startup leverages its manufacturing data to transition to a larger tier partner and slash unit production costs.

questions.text: Match each Supply Chain Financial Engineering lever to its tagline.
questions.explanation: C2C Cycle is Cycle Optimization, MOQ Strategy is Negotiation Strategies, and Component Obsolescence is handled by Modular BOM Design.

questions.text: In supply chain financial engineering, MOQ stands for Minimum Order ___.
questions.explanation: MOQ stands for Minimum Order Quantity.

questions.text: What does an MOQ strategy balance?
options: Founders' equity against government grant funding
Patent filing costs against trademark registration costs
Machine uptime against labor costs on the factory floor
The penalty of higher per-unit costs against the existential risk of tying up survival capital in mass inventory
questions.explanation: MOQ negotiation balances the penalty of higher per-unit costs against the existential risk of tying up survival capital in mass inventory.

questions.text: How does Modular BOM Design protect against component obsolescence?
options: It uses modular, alternative parts so that if a specific chip goes out of stock, the planning cycle does not freeze
It removes all electronic components from the design
It locks suppliers into rigid long-term contracts
It stockpiles years of every chip so shortages never happen
questions.explanation: A modular BOM with alternative parts means that if a specific chip goes out of stock, the entire production planning cycle does not freeze.

questions.text: In technopreneurship, PPC decisions directly dictate what?
questions.explanation: Supply Chain Financial Engineering & Capital Preservation: PPC decisions directly dictate cash runway, so material drops are synced with VC or crowdfunding cash flows.

questions.text: The Cash-to-Cash (C2C) Cycle is also known as the:
questions.explanation: The Cash-to-Cash (C2C) Cycle is also known as the Cash Conversion Cycle (CCC).

questions.text: What does the Cash-to-Cash (C2C) Cycle measure?
options: The number of units needed to cover all fixed overhead
The ratio of customer lifetime value to acquisition cost
The number of months a startup can survive at its current burn rate
The number of days it takes to convert cash outflows on materials or labor back into cash inflows from sales
questions.explanation: C2C measures the exact number of days it takes a startup to convert cash outflows (raw materials or manufacturing labor) back into cash inflows (revenue from customer sales).

questions.text: What is the formula for the C2C Cycle?
questions.explanation: C2C Cycle = DIO + DSO − DPO. Inventory days and receivable days are added; payable days are subtracted.

questions.text: Match each C2C component to its definition.
allChoices: Average days it takes to collect cash from customers after a sale
Average days raw parts, work-in-progress, and finished goods sit before being sold
Average days the startup takes to pay suppliers and contract manufacturers after an invoice

pairs.match: Average days raw parts, work-in-progress, and finished goods sit before being sold
Average days it takes to collect cash from customers after a sale
Average days the startup takes to pay suppliers and contract manufacturers after an invoice

questions.explanation: DIO covers inventory sitting before sale, DSO covers collecting from customers, and DPO covers paying suppliers. DIO and DSO are added to the cycle; DPO is subtracted.

questions.text: Which C2C component is subtracted from the cycle?
questions.explanation: DPO is subtracted. Taking longer to pay suppliers shortens the time your own cash is tied up.

questions.text: A startup's parts sit in inventory for 40 days (DIO), customers pay 15 days after a sale (DSO), and the startup pays suppliers 30 days after invoicing (DPO). What is its C2C Cycle?
questions.explanation: C2C = DIO + DSO − DPO = 40 + 15 − 30 = 25 days.

questions.text: A startup uses Just-In-Time parts that sit for 10 days (DIO), sells on a web store with immediate payment (DSO = 0), and has negotiated 30-day supplier terms (DPO). What is its C2C Cycle?
options: 0 days, since web store sales are immediate
20 days, a short but positive C2C
40 days, a long C2C where cash is trapped
-20 days, a negative C2C where cash is freed up immediately
questions.explanation: C2C = 10 + 0 − 30 = −20 days. A negative C2C is the technopreneurship goal: cash is freed up immediately.

questions.text: A startup moves from selling on its web store (immediate cash) to a retail store with 30-day payment terms. Which C2C component increases?
questions.explanation: DSO is the average number of days it takes to collect cash from customers after a sale. The source contrasts immediate cash on a web store with 30-day terms from a retail store.

questions.text: Negotiating deferred payments with suppliers lengthens the startup's C2C Cycle.
questions.explanation: Deferred payments increase DPO, which is subtracted in C2C = DIO + DSO − DPO, so the cycle gets shorter. Technopreneurship PPC negotiates deferred payments or structural staging for exactly this reason.

questions.text: Classify each sourcing practice as Traditional PPC (Cost Focus) or Technopreneurship PPC (Cash Focus).

pairs.term: Buys massive bulk orders to get a 10% unit discount
Buys smaller micro-batches to avoid locking up cash
Thousands of units sit in storage for months
Just-In-Time parts arrive right before assembly
Negotiates deferred payments or structural staging

questions.explanation: Traditional (cost focus): bulk orders for a 10% discount, high DIO, standard terms, long C2C. Technopreneurship (cash focus): micro-batches, low DIO with JIT parts, deferred payments, short or negative C2C.

questions.text: Under Traditional PPC's cost-focused sourcing, how long is cash typically trapped in the C2C cycle?
questions.explanation: Traditional PPC has a long C2C: cash is trapped for 90 to 120+ days. Technopreneurship aims for a short or negative C2C.

questions.text: How is the Traditional QC Model described?
options: Extended into real-world usage through IoT telemetry
Static and end-of-line, using statistical sampling at the end of a long assembly line
Agile and continuous, with a software and hardware feedback loop
In-line and automated at every critical assembly step
questions.explanation: The Traditional QC Model is static and end-of-line: it relies on frozen designs, strict mass-production tolerances, and statistical sampling at the end of a long assembly line.

questions.text: Why is end-of-line QC called "The Hardware Danger" for startups?
options: End-of-line testing slows machines below 90% capacity
Statistical sampling requires a Tier 1 manufacturer
A single software bug, uncalibrated sensor, or minor defect can ruin an entire batch, risking mass recalls or scrapped inventory
End-of-line testing is illegal for devices that use Bluetooth
questions.explanation: Waiting until the end of production creates a massive point of failure: one bug, uncalibrated sensor, or minor defect can ruin a batch and risk bankrupting the company through mass recalls or scrapped inventory.

questions.text: How is Technopreneurial QC described?
options: Static and end-of-line, relying on frozen product designs
Performed only by government facilities like DOST-AMCen
Limited to checking mechanical dimensions and cosmetic defects
Agile, continuous, and digitally integrated, with a software and hardware feedback loop catching flaws early
questions.explanation: Technopreneurial QC is an agile, continuous, digitally integrated quality management system with an active software and hardware feedback loop that catches flaws early, adapts to shifting designs, and preserves runway.

questions.text: What does HIL stand for in HIL Assembly Testing?
questions.explanation: HIL stands for Hardware-in-the-Loop assembly testing.

questions.text: Why does visual inspection fail for modern hardware devices?
options: Inspectors are not allowed to open sealed enclosures
Microscopes cannot see modern circuit boards clearly
Modern boards change color when they are defective
They are hybrid products with embedded firmware, so a board can look flawless yet the microcontroller may still fail to boot
questions.explanation: The Hybrid Challenge: devices combine physical components with embedded software or firmware. A circuit board might look visually flawless under a microscope, but the microcontroller could still fail to boot.

questions.text: What are the custom, automated test fixtures used in HIL testing often called?
questions.explanation: Technopreneurs design custom, automated test fixtures, often called "test beds" or "jigs", placed directly on the assembly line.

questions.text: Put the HIL Instant Diagnostics steps in order.
allChoices: Clamped: the assembled board is secured into the jig
Flashed & Tested: the jig flashes firmware and runs circuit diagnostics
On-Spot Rejection: failed parts are rejected

pairs.match: Clamped: the assembled board is secured into the jig
Flashed & Tested: the jig flashes firmware and runs circuit diagnostics
On-Spot Rejection: failed parts are rejected

questions.explanation: 1. Clamped, 2. Flashed & Tested, 3. On-Spot Rejection, before permanent housing installation.

questions.text: In HIL testing, when are failed parts rejected?
options: After the product ships to customers
Only during the yearly quality audit
At the end of the full production run
questions.explanation: On-Spot Rejection: failed parts are rejected before permanent housing installation.

questions.text: In traditional QC, what happens when a mid-production engineering change order (ECO) arrives?
options: The change is pushed to customers by IoT telemetry
The entire factory line halts to rewrite compliance rules
The change is ignored until the next product version
Test jigs update automatically with no halt
questions.explanation: Traditional QC halts the entire factory line to rewrite compliance rules. Technopreneurial QC uses cloud PLM so quality gates update without stopping production.

questions.text: Which example of an evolving design is given for mid-production ECOs?
questions.explanation: Product designs change constantly based on early customer feedback, for example swapping Bluetooth chips.

questions.text: In Dynamic ECOs, what does PLM stand for?
questions.explanation: Technopreneurial QC uses cloud-based Product Lifecycle Management (PLM) platforms.

questions.text: Which of the following are given as examples of cloud-based PLM platforms?
questions.explanation: OpenBOM and Propel are the cloud PLM examples. PCBWay and Protolabs are rapid fabrication services; Arduino and ESP32 appear in the local QC strategies.

questions.text: Put the Digital Thread (real-time sync) steps in order.
allChoices: Floor Sync: factory screens and test jigs update automatically
Instant Push: office changes push updated tolerances, schematics, and test specs
Zero Halts: quality gates update dynamically without stopping production

pairs.match: Instant Push: office changes push updated tolerances, schematics, and test specs
Floor Sync: factory screens and test jigs update automatically
Zero Halts: quality gates update dynamically without stopping production

questions.explanation: 1. Instant Push, 2. Floor Sync, 3. Zero Halts.

questions.text: Technopreneurial QC stops once the product leaves the factory dock.
questions.explanation: Beyond the Dock: technopreneurial QC doesn't stop when the product leaves the factory dock. It extends into real-world customer usage through post-purchase telemetry.

questions.text: Put the Closed-Loop QC (post-purchase telemetry) steps in order.
allChoices: Data Transmit: the device sends telemetry to the engineering cloud when turned on
Issue Detect: battery-drain or sensor calibration errors are caught in real-world use
PPC Update: the data modifies assembly/calibration for the next batch

pairs.match: Data Transmit: the device sends telemetry to the engineering cloud when turned on
Issue Detect: battery-drain or sensor calibration errors are caught in real-world use
PPC Update: the data modifies assembly/calibration for the next batch

questions.explanation: 1. Data Transmit, 2. Issue Detect, 3. PPC Update.

questions.text: Which issues are given as examples that post-purchase telemetry catches in real-world use?
questions.explanation: In Closed-Loop QC, battery-drain or sensor calibration errors are caught in real-world use, and the data immediately modifies assembly/calibration for the next batch.

questions.text: Classify each QC trait as Traditional Manufacturing QC or Technopreneurial PPC QC.

pairs.term: Fully frozen design; tolerances rarely change
Fluid and iterative design that evolves via ECOs
In-line and automated at every critical assembly step
Focus on mechanical dimensions and cosmetic defects
Focus on functional validation (firmware integration, signal integrity)
Defects discarded or manually reworked at a high cost
Rapid root-cause analysis with immediate software/line adjustment

questions.explanation: Traditional QC: frozen design, end-of-line sampling, mechanical/cosmetic focus, costly discard or rework. Technopreneurial QC: iterative design via ECOs, in-line automated testing, functional validation, rapid root-cause analysis.

questions.text: Which government facility is named as one a Filipino technopreneur might use when executing QC?
questions.explanation: Filipino technopreneurs may work with local Tier 3 contract manufacturers or government facilities like DOST-AMCen.

questions.text: To build custom testing jigs cheaply, startups pair open-source hardware with 3D-printed enclosures made where?
questions.explanation: Startups pair open-source hardware (like Arduinos or Raspberry Pis) with local 3D-printed enclosures made at a local DTI FabLab.

questions.text: Which open-source hardware is given as an example for building testing jigs?
questions.explanation: Startups frequently use open-source hardware like Arduinos or Raspberry Pis for testing jigs. ESP32 is the pre-certified RF module example.

questions.text: Where are the local manufacturers that startups hand their custom jigs to?
questions.explanation: Startups hand the custom jig directly to their local manufacturer in Laguna or Cavite to fully automate testing on the production line.

questions.text: In the Philippines, a device must be certified by the NTC if it uses which of the following?
questions.explanation: Any device using Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, or cellular networks must be certified by the National Telecommunications Commission (NTC).

questions.text: What does NTC stand for?
questions.explanation: NTC is the National Telecommunications Commission, which certifies devices that use Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, or cellular networks.

questions.text: How does Technopreneurial QC avoid failing NTC regulatory checks later?
options: By using pre-certified RF modules like the ESP32 during the DFM phase
By skipping certification for pilot runs under 100 units
By filing a utility model with IPOPHL first
By testing only at the end of the production line
questions.explanation: Technopreneurial QC factors certification into the timeline by using pre-certified RF modules (like ESP32) during the Design-For-Manufacturing phase.
